title: Muscle Memory for Agents: Compile not Merely Retrieve

analysis.tldr: Muscle Memory proposes compiling recurring user intent into quality-gated executable specialist agents instead of storing every pattern as text to retrieve and reinterpret at runtime.
analysis.problem: Retrieval-based personalization repeatedly asks a general orchestrator to reinterpret remembered preferences and procedures, so users can still pay a multi-turn tax for recurring tasks whose desired behavior is already stable.
analysis.core_idea: A Harvest→Analyze→Augment→Evaluate pipeline mines recurring task and behavioral patterns from conversation history, generates specialist mini-agents, validates them against source interactions, and triggers a specialist through a two-stage matcher when a future request fits its learned scope.

memory_design.write: Mine recurring intent from conversation history, separate task patterns from behavioral style, and compile sufficiently frequent/high-quality task patterns into executable specialist modules.
memory_design.organize: Store a user-specific library of specialist agents plus trigger metadata and a separate style profile rather than one retrieval corpus of textual memories.
memory_design.read: Route a new request by attribute/embedding matching plus a binary-questionnaire disambiguation stage, then invoke the matched specialist as its own task-specific LLM program.
memory_design.update_forget: The reference system regenerates and quality-filters specialists offline; it does not demonstrate continual online updating, conflict handling, or automatic retirement of stale specialists.

compared_to: retrieval-centric personalization where remembered instructions are inserted into a general orchestrator's context
skill/workflow memory that retrieves reusable text or procedures for the same controller to interpret
an unaugmented general assistant evaluated on the same held-out scenarios
analysis.evidence: The study builds history from 250 synthetic conversations across five personas and evaluates 90 held-out scenarios. A generated specialist fires in 36 cases and the augmented assistant wins 32 of those 36 comparisons (88.9%); the reported personalization score improves by 2.05 points on a 1–4 scale while accuracy falls by 0.28. Triggering remains imperfect: the paper reports 72% activation on similar scenarios and a 20% false-positive rate on different-domain scenarios.
analysis.why_it_matters: The design point is important even if the evidence is early: some mature procedural memory may be better represented as executable capability than as text that must be retrieved and reinterpreted every time.
limitations: The evaluation is synthetic: personas, histories, and held-out scenarios are generated rather than collected from long-lived real users.
Generation, matching, and judging rely heavily on the same Gemini model family, and no human evaluation is reported.
The paper does not establish a matched comparison against strong retrieval-based procedural-memory systems with equivalent specialist prompts and inference budget.
The compiled specialists are effectively static after generation; drift, conflict, revocation, and cross-user transfer remain open.
